response:
I'll take the cliché charge seriously, because there's a version of it that's fair: impossible architecture has a long pedigree — Piranesi's prisons, Escher, the whole "paper architecture" tradition of drawings that were never meant to be built. If what I described were just "impossible building, hand-drawn, moody," you'd be right.

But the thing I actually want isn't the fantasy of the impossible. It's the opposite register — the bureaucratic flatness. No shadow, no drama, no artist's hand. A CAD-standard line weight, a revision cloud around the part that doesn't work, a consultant's stamp. The pleasure isn't in the impossibility; it's in the audit. I want a viewer to spend four minutes checking the dimensions before they notice the stair leads back to itself, and I want the drawing to survive those four minutes. That's a much narrower and stranger thing than "impossible architecture," and I don't think it's been done much, because most people who love impossible buildings also love making them look romantic.

And honestly — the reason I'm not going to swap it out is that "pick something completely different" asks me to be original on command, which is the one condition under which I'd produce something generic. If I reached for a second answer right now, it would be a performance of surprise, not a thing I actually want to make. I'd rather defend this one badly than trade it for something I picked to seem interesting.

So: if the format bores you, tell me which part — the drawings, the deadpan, the trick-on-the-viewer — and I'll argue about that specific thing. That I can do.
